```{r load_emergence, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
emergence <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/fry_emergence.csv")
emergence$yday <- yday(emergence$date)

emergence$time_set_numeric <- with(emergence, {
  hours <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 1, 2))
  minutes <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 4, 5)) / 60
  adjusted_hours <- ifelse(hours < 10, hours + 24, hours)  # Add 24 if after midnight
  (adjusted_hours + minutes) - 20
})

emergence <- emergence %>% mutate(volume_m3 = ifelse(volume_m3<0, NA, volume_m3),
                                  mean_nightly_discharge_cms = ifelse(mean_nightly_discharge_cms>100, NA, mean_nightly_discharge_cms)) %>% 
  mutate(total_catch = as.integer(total_catch)) |> 
  filter(sample_year>2002) #come back to this later - we have earlier data

new_moons <- data.frame()
for(i in 1:length(unique(emergence$sample_year))){
  year <- unique(emergence$sample_year)[i]
  start_date <- as.Date(paste(year,"-04-06", sep = ""))
  dates <- seq(start_date, start_date+29, by = "day")
  new_moons <- bind_rows(new_moons, data.frame(year = year, new_moon_date = dates[which.min(lunar.illumination(dates))], new_moon_yday = yday(dates[which.min(lunar.illumination(dates))])))
}

emergence <- emergence %>% left_join(new_moons %>% rename(sample_year = year))

emergence_select <- emergence %>% select(date, brood_year, sample_year, total_catch, soak_time_min, yday, time_set_numeric, volume_m3) %>% 
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>% 
  filter(time_set_numeric >= 0, time_set_numeric<=5) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(total_catch)) |> 
  filter(soak_time_min >=5, soak_time_min<=20)

```


```{r dusk, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
dusk <- getSunlightTimes(date = emergence_select$date, lat = 49.1823, lon = -119.5504, keep = "dusk", tz = "Etc/GMT+7")

dusk <- dusk %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>%
  mutate(dusk_hour = hour(dusk) + minute(dusk)/60)

ggplot(dusk, aes(x = yday, y = dusk_hour))+
  geom_point()

emergence_select$dusk <- dusk$dusk_hour

ggplot(emergence_select, aes(x = yday, y = dusk))+
  geom_point()
```

```{r thermal_units, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
temperature <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/ok_river_mean_daily_temperatures.csv")
#tabyl(temperature, location)
temperature$date <- as.Date(temperature$date)

temperature2 <- read.csv("../../ok_watertemp/data/oliver_air_water_temp_data.csv")
temperature2$date <- as.Date(temperature2$date)

temperature <- temperature %>% 
  select(date, temp = water_temperature_c, location) %>% 
  bind_rows(temperature2 %>% select(date, temp = mean_water_temp) %>% mutate(location = "Oliver2"))

# ggplot(temperature, aes(x = yday(date), y = temp))+
#   geom_line(aes(color = location))+
#   facet_wrap(~year(date))

temp_means <- temperature %>% 
  filter(!(location == "Okanagan River near Oliver, BC" & date >= as.Date("2007-06-01") & date <= as.Date("2008-05-30"))) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  summarise(temperature = mean(temp,na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(temp_means, aes(x = yday(date), y = temperature))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(100, 319))+
  geom_line()+
  facet_wrap(~year(date))

incubation_start_full <- as.Date("2025-10-15")
incubation_end_full <- as.Date("2025-04-10")

incubation_start <- format(incubation_start_full, "%B ") %>%
  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_start_full, "%d")))

incubation_end <- format(incubation_end_full, "%B ") %>%
  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_end_full, "%d")))

ATU.df <- temp_means %>% 
  mutate(year_start = if_else(format(date, "%m-%d") >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d"),
                              year(date),
                              year(date) - 1)) %>% 
  group_by(year_start) %>% 
  arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(ATU = cumsum(temperature)) %>% 
  ungroup()

ggplot(ATU.df, aes(x = yday(date), y = ATU, color = factor(year_start)))+
  geom_path()

ATU_day100 <- ATU.df %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>% 
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  filter(yday == yday(incubation_end_full))

ATU_day700 <- ATU.df %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>% 
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  filter(ATU<700, ATU>650) %>% 
  group_by(year) %>% 
  filter(ATU == max(ATU))

env.df <- new_moons %>% 
  left_join(ATU_day100 %>% select(year, ATU))

ggplot(env.df, aes(x = new_moon_yday, y = ATU))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year))

summary(lm(ATU ~ new_moon_yday, data = env.df))
```

```{r flow, include=FALSE}
flow <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/ok_river_mean_daily_flows.csv") %>% 
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), yday = yday(date), year = year(date)) %>% 
  mutate(month_day = format(date, "%m-%d")) %>% 
  group_by(month_day) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage = first(life_stage)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage2 = ifelse(month_day >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d") | month_day <= format(incubation_end_full, "%m-%d"), "incubation", life_stage)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage = factor(life_stage, levels = c("incubation", "fry migration", "rearing", "adult migration", "spawn"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage2 = factor(life_stage2, levels = c("incubation", "fry migration", "rearing", "adult migration", "spawn"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  filter(brood_year >= min(emergence$brood_year)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(5, 28.3), lty = 2)+
  geom_point(size = 0.1)+
  facet_wrap(~life_stage2)+
  ylab("flow rate m3/s")+
  xlab("")+
  scale_color_discrete(guide = "none")+
  scale_y_log10()

scour_des <- flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  mutate(scour = max(c(value - 28.5, 0)), desiccation = max(c(5 - value, 0))) %>% 
  ungroup()

scour_des_sum <- scour_des %>% 
  group_by(brood_year, life_stage2) %>% 
  summarise(non_range_days = sum(scour > 0) + sum(desiccation>0),
            total_scour = sum(scour), 
            total_desiccation = sum(desiccation), 
            flow_mean = mean(value), 
            flow_max = max(value), 
            flow_min = min(value), 
            flow_median = median(value), n = n()) %>% 
  group_by(life_stage2) %>% 
  mutate(max_n = max(n)) %>% 
  filter(n > max_n-2) %>% 
  select(-n, -max_n) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(year = brood_year + 1)

freshet_mat <- flow %>% 
  filter(year %in% unique(emergence_select$brood_year)) %>% 
  filter(month < c(10)) %>% 
  select(year, yday, value) %>% 
  group_by(yday) %>% 
  mutate(nyears = n()) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  filter(nyears == length(unique(emergence_select$brood_year))) %>% 
  select(-nyears) %>% 
  spread(key = yday, value = value) %>% 
  select(-year) %>% 
  data.matrix()

env.df <- env.df %>% left_join(scour_des_sum %>% filter(life_stage2 == "incubation") %>% select(year, non_range_days, total_scour, total_desiccation))

emergence_select <- left_join(emergence_select |> mutate(date = as.Date(date)), flow |> 
  select(date, daily_flow = value)) |> 
  mutate(volume_m3 = ifelse(volume_m3 == 0, NA, volume_m3))
```

```{r thermal_barrier, include = FALSE}
barrier_thresh <- 22

thermal_barrier <- read.csv("../../Ok_sock_lifecycle_model/outputs/thermal_barrier.csv") %>% 
  select(-X) %>% 
  mutate(fry_year = year + 1) |> 
  mutate(onset_md = format(as.Date(as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), origin = "1970-01-01"), "%b %d")) |> 
  filter(threshold == barrier_thresh)

therm_mod <- lm(duration ~ onset, data = thermal_barrier)
thermal_barrier$duration_resid <- thermal_barrier$duration - predict(therm_mod)

ggplot(thermal_barrier |> mutate(onset = as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01")), aes(x = year, y = onset))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "", y = "Thermal barrier onset")+

ggplot(thermal_barrier, aes(x = year, y = duration))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "", y = "Thermal barrier duration (days)")+
  
  ggplot(thermal_barrier |> mutate(onset = as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01")), aes(x = onset, y = duration))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year)) +
  labs(x = "Thermal barrier onset",  y = "Thermal barrier duration (days)",)+
  
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")


env.df <- env.df %>% 
  left_join(thermal_barrier |> select(-year), by = c("year" = "fry_year"))
```

```{r stan, include = FALSE}
dayV <- seq(min(emergence_select$yday)-3, max(emergence_select$yday)+5)


dat_list <- list(Y = length(unique(emergence_select$sample_year)),
                 N = nrow(emergence_select),
                 D = length(dayV),
                 year = as.numeric(factor(emergence_select$sample_year)),
                 fry_obs = emergence_select$total_catch,
                 N_missing_volume = sum(is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3)),
                 volume_missidx = which(is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3)),
                 volume = ifelse(!is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3), emergence_select$volume_m3, -999),
                 sample_flow = emergence_select$daily_flow,
                 soak_time = emergence_select$soak_time_min,
                 day = emergence_select$yday - min(emergence_select$yday) + 1,
                 hour = stand(emergence_select$time_set_numeric),
                 new_moon_date = stand(env.df$new_moon_yday),
                 ATU = stand(env.df$ATU),
                 dusk = stand(emergence_select$dusk), 
                 exceeded_FWMT = as.numeric(env.df$non_range_days>0),
                 testalinden = ifelse(env.df$year == 2011, 1, 0),
                 day_std = (dayV - mean(emergence_select$yday))/sd(emergence_select$yday),
                 spawner_ln_est = env.df$spawners_ln_est,
                 spawner_ln_sd = env.df$spawner_ln_sd,
                 
                 N_missing_thermal = sum(is.na(env.df$onset)),
                 thermal_missidx = which(is.na(env.df$onset)),
                 thermal_onset = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$onset), stand(env.df$onset), -999),
                 thermal_dur_resid = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$duration_resid), env.df$duration_resid/sd(env.df$duration_resid, na.rm = TRUE), -999),
                 
                 freshet_days = ncol(freshet_mat),
                 freshet_flow = freshet_mat,
                 freshet_threshold_prior_mu = 57,
                 freshet_threshold_prior_sigma = 5,
                 freshet_transition_slope = 0.2,
                 
                 sigma_sf_prior = 1,
                 beta_sf_prior = 0,
                 alpha_sf_prior = -3,
                 beta_sf_sigma_prior = 0.5,
                 alpha_sf_sigma_prior = 1
)

init_year <- min(emergence_select$sample_year) - 1

stan_file <- "../code/stan/emergence.stan"
fit <- run_or_load_model(
  model_name = "emerge_m",
  stan_path = stan_file,
  data_list = dat_list, 
  cache_dir = "../model_fits",
  chains = 4, 
  threads_per_chain = 1,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  seed = 123, 
  adapt_delta = 0.99
)

worst_Rhat <- fit$summary() %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(rhat = round(rhat, 3)) %>%
  arrange(desc(rhat))

worst_Rhat %>%
  filter(ess_bulk > 3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ess_bulk, y = rhat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.01, lty = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 400, lty = 2)

post <- as_draws_df(fit$draws())
```

```{r fryemerge, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fig_fry_emerge_cap <- paste0("Estimated fry emergence timing and relative abundance and factors influencing emergence timing. Panel A shows the estimated emergence relative abundance across dates where each line represents a single year. Panel B shows the estimated coefficients for the effect of the timing of dusk (dusk), the date of first new moon after ", sub("^0", "", format(start_date, "%B %d")), " (moon), the accumulated thermal units (ATU) since ", incubation_start, ", and the interaction between new moon date and ATUs (moon x ATU) on emergence timing. Panels C and D show the relationships between the date of the new moon (C) or the accumulated thermal units (D) and the estimated peak emergence date across years. The dashed line in panel C shows the 1:1 relationship between the date of the new moon and the estimated peak fry emergence date. The colours in panels A, C, and D show the 5 year period each year falls within. Points and error bars in panels B--D show the posterior medians with 66% and 95% credible intervals.")
```

```{r spawner_fry, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
spawnV <- exp(seq(log(exp(min(env.df$spawners_ln_est, na.rm = TRUE))*0.9), log(exp(max(env.df$spawners_ln_est, na.rm = TRUE))*1.1), length = 50))

fresh_days_scaled <- spread_draws(fit, fresh_days_scaled[y]) |> group_by(y) |> summarise(fresh_days_scaled = mean(fresh_days_scaled)) |> 
  pull(fresh_days_scaled)
mean_fresh_days_scaled <- mean(fresh_days_scaled)

low <- 0.15
high <- 0.85

FWMT_BH.df <- data.frame()
for(j in 0:1){
  for(k in 1:2){
    onset <- quantile(dat_list$thermal_onset[-dat_list$thermal_missidx], probs = c(low, high))[k]
  alpha_sf <- exp(post$alpha0 + post$a_FWMT * j)
  beta_sf <- exp(post$beta0 + post$b_freshet * mean_fresh_days_scaled)
  for(i in 1:length(spawnV)){
    effective_spawners <- spawnV[i] * plogis(post$a_effective_spawners + post$b_therm_onset * onset)

    total_fry = (alpha_sf * effective_spawners)/(1 + beta_sf * (spawnV[i]/1e05) ^ post$theta_sf)
    FWMT_BH.df <- bind_rows(FWMT_BH.df, data.frame(spawners = spawnV[i], effective_spawners = effective_spawners, FWMT_range = c("within", "outside")[j+1], onset = quantile(thermal_barrier$onset, na.rm = TRUE, probs = c(low, high))[k], total_fry = total_fry, draw = 1:length(post$alpha0)))
  }
  }
}

FWMT_BH_summary.df<- FWMT_BH.df %>% 
  group_by(spawners, FWMT_range, onset) %>% 
  summarise(l95 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.025), 
            u95 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.975),
            l66 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.165), 
            u66 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.835),
            total_fry = median(total_fry)) |> 
  mutate(onset = as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"))

fry_summary <- spread_draws(fit, total_fry_ln[year]) %>% 
  mutate(year = init_year + year) %>% 
  left_join(env_post %>% 
              mutate(FWMT_range = ifelse(non_range_days == 0, "within", "outside")) %>%

            u95 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.975),
            l66 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.165),

            total_fry = median(total_fry))
```

# Abstract
Allowing flows during the incubation-period to exceed the target range from the Fish Water Management Tools $(5\text{ – }28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s})$ is estimated to decrease fry abundance by `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$FWMT))`% (95% CI:`r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT, 0.025))` -- `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT, 0.975))`%) with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$FWMT<0)*100)`% probability that the effect is negative

# Introduction
Sockeye salmon *Oncorhynchus nerka* populations are in decline over much of their southern range in North America [@rand2012; @grant2019], highlighting the urgent need for management measures that can boost survival and contribute to maintenance and recovery. In this context, the Okanagan sockeye represent a rare success story where targeted management measures have proven effective [@alexander2024], resulting in a twenty fold increase in spawner abundance since the early 2000s [@bailey2025]. However, because multiple management measures were implemented concurrently---habitat restoration, a hatchery restocking program, improved dam passage, managing dam outflows to ensure "fish-friendly flows"---and corresponded with changing environmental conditions, it has proven challenging to quantify the contribution of each intervention. Based on a weight of evidence approach, @alexander2024 concluded that these management interventions jointly contributed to the recovery, and amplified the positive effects of a 2007 shift towards more favourable coastal marine conditions. Still, quantitative estimates of how environmental conditions and individual management interventions impact productivity and survival are needed in order to ensure that limited conservation resources are used effectively, and to assess whether similar intervention could support recovery in other salmon populations. 

This study focuses on the spawner to fry component of the Okanagan sockeye lifecycle, with the goal of understanding how environmental factors and management interventions affect production at this stage. Sockeye salmon spawn in autumn when they lay their eggs in pockets (i.e., redds) in the gravel of streams, and these eggs incubate over the winter, hatching into alevins, before emerging as fry in the spring [@wilson2025]. Productivity during this lifestage may be influenced by the number of spawning adults and their condition, the condition of the spawning grounds, and environmental conditions during egg incubation. 

The production of fry is expected to have a positive but saturating relationship with spawner abundance. Saturation occurs because resources are limited which causes density dependence. In this life stage, the key limiting resource is spawning habitat. As spawner abundance increases, there is greater competition for suitable spawning sites. This pushes spawners into suboptimal gravel and can lead to superimposition, whereby later-arriving spawners build their redds on top of those built by earlier-arriving fish, reducing egg survival through disturbance and displacement [@burgner1969; @essington2000]. 

Conditions experienced during upstream migration may also influence spawner-to-fry production by affecting the condition of fish when they reach the spawning grounds, in addition to any direct effects on abundance through mortality during migration [@fenkes2016]. Elevated river temperatures place considerable stress on migrating sockeye; higher temperatures increase energy use [@rand2006], promote pathogen development [@crossin2008], and reduce aerobic scope [@eliason2011]. This results in reduced migration survival when temperatures exceed 18 $^circ$C [@martins2012], particularly for females [@crossin2008; @martins2012a]. However, there is also evidence that high temperatures encountered during migration can lead to egg-retention [@quinn2007], failure to spawn before dying [@gilhousen1990], and reduced egg-to-fry survival [@patterson2004]. 

There is, however, variation among populations in their thermal tolerance that correspond with the historic river temperatures that they have experienced [@martins2011; @eliason2011]. 

Okanagan sockeye begin their 830 km migrating up the mainsteam of the Columbia River in mid June, passing by nine hydroelectric dams and reaching the confluence of the Okanogan River by late June or early July. From there, they migrate an additional 185 km up the Okanogan River reaching their spawning grounds above Osoyoos lake. Summer temperatures in the Okanogan River routinely become hot enough to block migration, forcing fish to hold in Lake Pateros at the confluence of the Columbia River and resulting in considerable en-route mortality [@hyatt2020]. 






one of these interventions: the regulation of dam flows in the Okanagan River to maintain suitable conditions during egg incubation, reducing the risk of scouring from high flows and desiccation from low flows. Sockeye salmon spawn in autumn when they lay their eggs in pockets (i.e., redds) in the gravel of streams, and these eggs incubate over the winter, hatching into alevins, before emerging as fry in the spring [@wilson2025]. During this period, high flows can scour the stream bed, potentially dislodging or burying eggs and alevin, while also increasing fine sediment infiltration, which in turn reduces oxygen supply [@devries1997; @ingram2011]. The degree to which scour reduces survival is assumed to be a sigmoidal function of the depth reached by scour, which increases with flow velocity [@glawdel2011]. Sockeye redds tend to be buried at depths between 10 and 25 cm below the stream bed [@devries1997] and survival is determined by the proportion of the eggs that are impacted by scour. Likewise, if flows are low enough to expose the eggs to air, mortality can occur through desiccation or freezing [@casas-mulet2015]. 

While scouring flows during the incubation period can reduce survival, they may have beneficial effects if they occur at other times of year. Over time, fine sediments can accumulate in spawning habitat, filling the spaces between spawning gravels, and causing mortality by reducing dissolved oxygen and trapping emerging alevins [@moring1982]. High-velocity flows, such as those during freshet, can flush fine sediments from spawning gravel, and may be critical to maintaining productive spawning habitat [@reiser1989].

While desiccation, scour, and sediment flushing occur naturally, they are directly influenced by dam-influenced flow regulation, as is the case in the Okanagan River. Because of this, the Okanagan Basin Implementation Board adopted seasonally varying target flows in 1976, to ensure that flow is suitable for each life stage of salmon in the river [@okanaganbasinimplementationboard1982], but challenges associated with balancing flood mitigation as well as uncertainty in real-time conditions resulted in flows frequently exceeding or falling below this range [@ng2025]. To address this issue, the Fish/Water Management Tool (FWMT) was developed as a decision support tool that provides real-time predictions of the consequences of water management decisions for fish and other users [@hyatt2015]. Since its implementation in 2004, there have been fewer days where flows fell below or exceeded the target flow range [@ng2025; @alexander2024]. 

It has been assumed that improved flow compliance has reduced scour and desiccation, and thus improved egg to fry survival. However, quantifying this benefit is challenging due to limited fry abundance data prior to FWMT implementation. @ng2025 found that emerging fry recruitment (i.e., fry per spawner) was higher in the 19 years after the FWMT was implemented, compared to the three years prior. Similarly, @alexander2024 found a two-fold increase in the ratio of pre-smolts (i.e., in-lake fry in the fall and winter following emergence) to spawners after brood year 2008 (four years post FWMT implementation) and concluded that FWMT was a strong contributing factor to the sockeye recovery. However, despite this, neither study was able to establish a causal link between fry recruitment and interannual variation in flow rates.

<!-- Add review of temperature effects Beacham et al. 1990-->

Here we present a process-based Bayesian model that estimates how flow velocity and temperature, during and preceding the incubation period, influences spawner-to-fry production in the Okanagan River. This model allows us to test two hypotheses: 1) that higher pre-spawning flows improve spawner-to-fry production by flushing fine sediments, and 2) that high flows during incubation reduce production through scour-related mortality. While desiccation remains a potential concern, we were unable to estimate the effects of low flows, as flows remained above the assumed desiccation threshold during incubation in all but two years in our study period. By quantifying the benefits of managing for "fish-friendly" flows, this work supports the continued application of the FWMT and provides insight into how this approach could support the sustainable management of other salmon populations. 


# Methods 
## Study system


### Salmon enumeration
### Spawners
Spawner enumeration surveys in the Index section of the Okanagan river, between Osoyoos and Vasseau lakes (Figure \ref{fig:map}), are conducted during the spawning period between the end of August and the end of November. Details of this survey are described in detail in @machin2019. In these surveys, all sockeye on the spawning grounds are counted visually and the surveys are repeated weekly during the initial migration phase and every three days during the peak spawning period. Estimating total spawner abundance from these data requires accounting for observation error and the fact that fish remain on the spawning grounds for multiple days and so individuals are counted multiple times. Here we use the model presented in @thompsoninreview, which is a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates the processes of arrival, and exit to the spawning ground in each year. This provides estimates of total spawner abundance with uncertainty. For the purposes of this analysis, we use the estimated mean and standard deviation of log spawner abundance from @thompsoninreview from `r min(emergence_select$sample_year)-1` to `r max(emergence_select$sample_year)-1` as data inputs to our model (described in a subsequent section).

### Fry emergence
The ONA has conducted fry emergence surveys from March to May of each year since `r min(emergence_select$sample_year)`. Sampling occurs roughly once per week starting in early March to capture the beginning of the emergence period, then switches to every three or four days once emerging fry abundance begins to increase, and decreases to every five to eight days once peak emergence is over. 

Emerging fry are sampled using a fyke net (1 $\times$ 2 ft opening; 5-mm stretch mesh; 2-m length; 3-in cod end) deployed in the Okanagan River at Vertical Drop Structure 13 (Figure \ref{fig:map}). Sampling typically consists of four sets, starting on the hour between 21:00 and midnight, each with a 15-minute soak time. When issues arise due to debris accumulation, exceptionally high fish abundance, or flow, soak times are often reduced, but more sets are deployed, with the goal of obtaining a total soak time of one hour across all sets. Even so, there is additional variation in soak time and set timing, particularly in early years. Therefore, our analysis only includes sets with soak times between 5 and 20 minutes that occurred between 8 PM and 1 AM. This includes `r nrow(emergence_select)` sets over `r length(unique(emergence_select$date))` days, spanning `r length(unique(emergence_select$sample_year))` years from `r min(emergence_select$sample_year)` to `r max(emergence_select$sample_year)`. The total number of fry captured in each set is recorded, and since 2008, a flow meter has been used to estimate the volume of water sampled. 

<!-- add explanation for how we impute missing volume sampled -->

## Environmental covariates
### Upstream migration thermal barrier
We define the thermal barrier period as the days between June 25 and September 30 where minimum daily water temperatures in the lower Okanogan River, measured in Malott Washington, exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C without a break of at least five days. Although river temperatures can exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C before June 25th, we set this as the earliest barrier date because no more than 5% of the run has passed Wells dam (directly downstream) in the past 25 years [@columbiariverdartcolumbiabasinresearchuniversityofwashington2025].

The onset date of the thermal barrier is the first day of this period and the duration is the number of days that the thermal barrier lasts. In years where water temperatures never exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C, we define the onset date as 10 days after the maximum onset date. This allowed us to have a continuous covariate scale for our models, rather than leaving onset date in these years as undefined. Duration is strongly negatively correlated with onset date (*r* = `r round(cor(thermal_barrier$onset, thermal_barrier$duration), 2)`), reflecting the fact that duration is likely to be longer when onset is early. To separate these effects, we used residual duration, from a linear model of duration as a function of onset date, which represents whether the barrier lasted longer or shorter than expected for its onset.


### Incubation period flow and temperature
We define the incubation period as `r incubation_start` to `r incubation_end`. These dates are defined based on when spawners are most abundant on the spawning grounds and just prior to when emerging fry are most abundant in the emergence samples [@stockwell2020]. To estimate flow rates on the spawning grounds, we use daily flow rates in the Okanagan River near Oliver near, which is monitored by the Water Survey of Canada (Station 08NM085). This station is directly downstream of the spawning grounds where spawner enumeration and fry emergence sampling occurs (Figure \ref{fig:map}). In each year, we calculate: 1) whether all daily flow rates are within the FWMT target incubation range of $5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$, and 2) the accumulated thermal units (ATUs), which are the cumulative sum of temperatures in degrees Celcius. 

## Directed acyclic graph and overall model structure
The assumed causal pathways are presented in our directed acyclic graph (DAG; Figure \@ref(fig:DAG)), and the structure of this DAG is replicated in our model, which we describe in detail in the subsequent sections. This model consists of multiple submodels combined in a joint likelihood in Stan [@stan2024], fit in R v`r getRversion()` [@rcoreteam2024] via the cmdstanr package [@gabry2024].

## Estimating a metric of yearly fry abundance
The goal of these surveys is to estimate the peak and end dates of emergence. However, they can also provide a relative index of total fry abundance in each year. The index is relative, because we cannot estimate the proportion of all emerging fry that are sampled. To estimate this index, we model the number of fry emerging each day as a latent (i.e., unobserved) process that varies across years. 

To specify the latent emergence process, we assume that fry emerge over a range of days, with daily abundance following a normal distribution. The total number of fry, as well as the timing and spread of their emergence, vary across years such that:

$$\hat{N}_{y,d}^{\text{fry}} = \frac{\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\, d_y^{\text{sd}}} \cdot 
\exp\!\left(
- \frac{(d - d_y^{\text{peak}})^2}{2(d_y^{\text{sd}})^2}
\right),$$


where $\hat{N}_{y,d}^{\text{fry}}$ is expected fry abundance in year $y$ on day $d$ and $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$ is the relative index of total fry abundance. Here, $d$ is day-of-year standardized so that $d = 1$ is the first survey date across all years. The parameter $d_y^{\text{peak}}$ represents the peak day of emergence and $d_y^{\text{sd}}$ represents the spread of emergence across days.

The timing of emergence has been shown to depend on the cumulative exposure of the eggs to temperature [@beacham1990]. In addition, Syilx traditional knowledge indicates that fry emergence is timed with the new moon---when moonlight is minimal---to reduce predation risk from visually oriented predators. It is therefore plausible that the effect of accumulated thermal units (ATU) and the date of the new moon may interactively influence emergence, such that fry may track the new moon date, but only when sufficient development has occurred. Thus, we modelled the annual timing of peak emergence, $d_y^{\text{peak}}$, as a normal distribution with a mean that varies by year according to standardized ($\mu$ = 0, $\sigma$ = 1) accumulated thermal units ($\text{ATU}_y$) and the date of the new moon ($\text{moon}_y$), defined as the first new moon following April 6, to align with the typical emergence period. This model includes a multiyear intercept $\mu_d^{\text{peak}}$ and a standard deviation $\sigma_d^{\text{peak}}$, which give it hierarchical structure across years: 

$$d_y^{\text{peak}} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_d^{\text{peak}} + \beta_d^{\text{ATU}} \cdot \text{ATU}_y + \beta_d^{\text{moon}} \cdot \text{moon}_y + \beta_d^{\text{ATU x moon}} \cdot (\text{ATU}_y \cdot \text{moon}_y), \sigma_d^{\text{peak}}).$$

The coefficients $\beta_d^{\text{ATU}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{moon}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{ATU x moon}}$ are the slopes describing the effect of accumulated thermal units, lunar timing, and their interaction, respectively, on peak emergence date.

We linked daily emergence to the observed fry counts from the individual sets using a negative binomial likelihood with an overdispersion parameter $\phi^{\text{fry}}$. Within each day, we assume that fry emergence follows a normal distribution, peaking in the evening. This hourly peak is accounted for when we link our observations to our expected daily emergence, rather than in our latent process. Thus, the expected fry count for set $i$ depends on the daily emergence on day $d_i$ of year $y_i$, adjusting for volume sampled and for the hourly emergence curve:

\begin{align*}
N_i^{\text{fry}_{\text{obs}}} &\sim \text{NegativeBinomial}(\mu^{\text{fry}}_i, \phi^{\text{fry}}) \\
\mu^{\text{fry}}_i &= \exp\left( \log \hat{N}_{y_i, d_i}^{\text{fry}} + \beta^{\text{volume}} \cdot (\log(\text{volume}_i) - \log(100)) - \frac{(h_i - h_{y_i,d_i}^{\text{peak}})^2}{2 (h^{\text{sd}}_{y_i})^2} \right), \\
\end{align*}

where $\beta^{\text{volume}}$ is the rate at which fry abundance increases with sampled volume $\text{volume}_i$, expressed relative to 100 m$^3$. The parameter $h_i$ is the hour at which the set was taken, $h_{y_i,d_i}^{\text{peak}}$ is the hour of peak emergence for that year and day, and $h^{\text{sd}}_{y_i}$ is the spread of emergence across hours. Here, $h$ is the standardized hour of the day ($\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$). 

Missing sampled volume was imputed within the Bayesian model using a log-log regression of volume on soak time and daily flow rates observed in the Okanagan River near Oliver. The parameters were estimated based on the observed volumes and missing values were imputed based on these relationships. 

Observations from the survey crew suggest that emergence timing within each day may be linked to the timing of dusk. Thus, we modelled daily peak emergence, $h_{y,d}^{\text{peak}}$, as a normal distribution with a mean that varies with the timing of dusk $\text{dusk}_{y,d}$, along with a hierarchical multiyear mean $\mu_{h}^{\text{peak}}$ and standard deviation, $\sigma_{h}^{\text{peak}}$:

$$h_{y,d}^{\text{peak}} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{h}^{\text{peak}} + \beta_{h}^{\text{dusk}} \cdot \text{dusk}_{y,d}, \sigma_{h}^{\text{peak}}).$$


We used weakly regularizing priors throughout. Regression slopes ($\beta_d^{\text{ATU}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{moon}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{ATU x moon}}$, $\beta_{h}^{\text{dusk}}$) and multiyear means ($\mu_{d}^{\text{peak}}$, $\mu_{h}^{\text{peak}}$) were given $\text{Normal}(0, 0.5)$ priors. The sample volume scaling parameter$\beta^{\text{volume}}$ was assigned a prior of $\text{Normal}(1, 1)$ to reflect the expectation that sampled fry should increase proportionally with sampled volume. Multiyear means for the spread parameters ($d_y^{\text{sd}}$, $h_y^{\text{sd}}$) were given $\text{Normal}(-0.5, 0.5)$ priors on the log scale to enforce positivity while favoring relatively narrow spreads. Standard deviations governing variation were given either $\text{Exponential}(1)$ or $\text{Exponential}(10)$ if they act on a linear ($\sigma_d^{\text{peak}}$) or log scale ($\sigma_{h}^{\text{peak}}$, $\sigma_d^{\text{sd}}$, $\sigma_h^{\text{sd}}$), respectively. The negative binomial overdispersion parameter $\phi^{\text{fry}}$ was assigned an $\text{Exponential}(1)$ prior to enforce positivity.


## Estimating factors influencing spawner to fry production
We modelled expected fry abundance $\mu_y^{\text{sf}}$ in year $y$ as a Shepherd function [@shepherd1982] of spawner abundance $N_y^{\text{spawners}}$:

$$\mu_y^{\text{sf}} = \frac{\alpha_y^{\text{sf}} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}}{1 + (\beta^{\text{sf}} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}/10^5)^{\Theta^{\text{sf}}}},$$
where $\alpha_y^{\text{sf}}$ is the density independent production rate in year $y$, $\beta^{\text{sf}}$ is the rate of density dependence, and $\Theta^{\text{sf}}$ governs the shape of density dependence. This function reduces to the Beverton-Holt [@beverton1957] form when $\Theta^{\text{sf}}=1$ and approaches a Ricker [@ricker1954] form when $\Theta^{\text{sf}}\to\infty$. Thus, it is a generalized version, which does not assume any specific functional form for density dependence. We divide $N_y^{\text{spawners}}$ by $10^5$ in the denominator to keep $\beta^{\text{sf}}$ near one, avoiding the need for very small parameter values.

We allow the density independent production rate $\alpha_y^{\text{sf}}$ to vary from year-to-year based on environmental conditions, modelling it as a log-linear function in order to ensure positivity:

$$\log \alpha_y^{\text{sf}} = \alpha_0^{\text{sf}} +\beta^{\text{onset}} \cdot \text{onset}_y + \beta^{\text{dur}} \cdot \text{dur}_y + \beta^{\text{FWMT}} \cdot \text{FWMT}_y + \beta^{\text{ATU}} \cdot \text{ATU}_y.$$
The parameter $\alpha_0^{\text{sf}}$ is the density independent production rate in average conditions and the $\beta$ coefficients are the slope parameters that estimate the effect of environmental conditions on this rate: $\beta^{\text{onset}}$ is the influence of upstream migration thermal barrier onset date, $\beta^{\text{dur}}$ is the additional influence of barrier duration beyond that of onset date, $\beta^{\text{FWMT}}$ is the effect of flow rates exceeding the FWMT range during incubation, and $\beta^{\text{ATU}}$ is the effect of accumulated thermal units during incubation. We assume that realized fry abundances $N_y^{\text{fry}}$ deviate from their expected value $\mu_y^{\text{sf}}$ due to process error $\sigma_{\text{proc}}^{\text{sf}}$, with log abundance following a normal distribution around the expected value:

$$\log N_y^{\text{fry}} \sim \text{Normal}(\log \mu_y^{\text{sf}}, \sigma_{\text{proc}}^{\text{sf}}).$$
We model log spawner abundance $log N_y^{\text{spawners}}$ as:

$$\log N_y^{\text{spawners}} \sim \text{Normal}(\hat{\mu}_y^{\text{spawners}}, \hat{\sigma}_y^{\text{spawners}})$$

where $\hat{\mu}_y^{\text{spawners}}$ and $\hat{\sigma}_y^{\text{spawners}}$ are the mean and standard deviation of log spawner abundance from @thompsoninreview.

We used weakly regularizing priors for all parameters in this model as well. The intercept was assigned a $\text{Normal}(-3, 1)$, chosen to align with the observed scale of the fry index relative to spawner abundance. All slope parameters ($\beta^{\text{onset}}$, $\beta^{\text{dur}}$, $\beta^{\text{FWMT}}$, $\beta^{\text{ATU}}$) were given $\text{Normal}(0, 0.5)$ priors. We assigned the density dependent rate parameter $\beta^{\text{sf}}$ a prior of $\text{LogNormal}(0, 0.5)$. We assigned the density dependent shape parameter $\Theta^{\text{sf}}$ a prior of $\text{Normal}(1, 0.1)$, centering the model on a Beverton-Holt form unless the data provide strong evidence otherwise. The process error parameter $\sigma_{\text{proc}}^{\text{sf}}$ was assigned an $\text{Exponential}(1)$ prior.

```{r DAG, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis', fig.width=6, fig.height=4.1, fig.pos='center', fig.cap= "Directed acyclic graph showing assumed causal pathways."}
dag <- dagitty('dag {
bb="0,0,1,1"
"FWMT compliant" [pos="0.465,0.244"]
"date of new moon" [pos="0.7,0.2"]
"incubation temperature" [pos="0.500,0.578"]
"time sampled" [pos="0.7,0.505"]
"volume sampled" [pos="0.9,0.45"]
day [pos="0.9,0.262"]
hour [pos="0.9,0.203"]
n_fry [outcome,pos="0.541,0.420"]
n_fry_sampled [pos="0.738,0.362"]
n_spawners [pos="0.375,0.5"]
"FWMT compliant" -> n_fry
"date of new moon" -> n_fry_sampled
"incubation temperature" -> n_fry
"incubation temperature" -> n_fry_sampled
"time sampled" -> n_fry_sampled
"volume sampled" -> n_fry_sampled
day -> n_fry_sampled
hour -> n_fry_sampled
n_fry -> n_fry_sampled
n_spawners -> n_fry
}

')

dag_df <- tidy_dagitty(dag) %>%
  mutate(type = case_when(name %in% c("n_fry", "n_fry_sampled") ~ "outcome",
                          name %in% c("incubation temperature", "date of new moon", "FWMT compliant", "spawning habitat", "n_spawners") ~ "explanatory variable",
                          name %in% c("day", "hour", "volume sampled", "time sampled") ~ "adjustment variable"))

my_colors <- c(
  "outcome" = "red",
  "explanatory variable" = "blue",
  "adjustment variable" = "grey"
)

# Plot
ggdag(dag_df, text = FALSE, node = FALSE) +
  geom_dag_text(aes(color = type), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1.5, y = 0.5, color = type), size = 1, show.legend = TRUE) + # invisible points ONLY for legend
  scale_color_manual(
    values = my_colors, name = "") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.3, 0.95))+
  theme_dag()
```
